ai_industry.title: AMD Zen 6 EPYC ‘Venice’ deep dive and benchmarking
ai_industry.summary_original: AMD has pulled back the curtain on its Zen 6 microarchitecture. We deep-dive into the differences between Zen 5 and 6, as well as detail our first benchmarks of AMD’s Venice CPUs.
ai_industry.content_original:
AMD Zen 6 EPYC ‘Venice’ deep dive and benchmarking – 9686F outclasses Nvidia’s Vera, dual EPYC 9996 with 1,024 threads delivers up to 93% performance gain gen-on-gen
Our first look at Zen 6, both under the hood and in real-world applications.
AMD’s EPYC ‘Venice’ CPUs are the first to debut the new Zen 6 architecture, and we’ve been testing two chips from the range over the past several weeks to see how they compare to Nvidia’s Vera, and more broadly, how the Zen 6 architecture departs from Zen 5 ahead of the expected consumer-focused Olympic Ridge launch next year. Zen 5 was a ground-up redesign of AMD’s storied Zen core, and Zen 6 takes that foundation and expands it in just about every regard.
Zen 6 uses TSMC’s N2P node, but it also comes with significant architectural changes under the hood. Within the core, a redesigned vector engine pushes AMD’s SIMD performance even higher, and it now natively supports half-precision FP16 instructions alongside full, 32-bit precision. It also splits integer schedulers within the execution engine, allowing for more instructions in flight through the core.
Across the die, AMD made other significant changes. The single IOD of previous generations is now split across two IODs, giving the SP7 platform access to 16 memory channels (though at the cost of PCIe 6.0 lanes compared to the previous generation and SP8 platform).
The CCDs have been upgraded, too, for the first time since Zen 3. A standard Zen 6 CCD can now scale up to 12 cores, while a Zen 6c packs 32 cores. With Zen 5 and 5c, CCDs topped out at eight cores and 16 cores, respectively. For the Zen 6c CCD, AMD also doubled the amount of shared L3 per core, which effectively quadruples the L3 compared to Zen 5c, since the CCD packs twice the number of cores.
Interestingly, Zen 6 is neither a marginal optimization to Zen 5, nor a complete architecture redesign. Stepping back, it looks like AMD pushes as many dials as it has access to to their highest level, and that holds up looking at performance.
The 256-core EPYC 9996 delivers 1,024 threads in a 2P configuration, which came out 93% ahead of the 768-thread 2P EPYC 9965 server we tested in SPEC CPU 2026’s intrate throughput test. The frequency-optimized EPYC 9686F excels elsewhere, notably in scientific computing and HPC workloads, and it serves as AMD’s competitor to Vera, at least before the LPDDR-based Verano platform arrives from AMD next year.
AMD says it believes Venice is fundamentally a generation ahead of the competition, which would be a worthless line if it wasn’t backed up by data. Intel’s Granite Rapids-AP is rarely in the conversation, and although Vera maintains some competitive positions, Venice is often ahead — sometimes orders of magnitude ahead.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Intel’s Diamond Rapids is set to launch next year, which should help balance the scales. But AMD has set an incredibly high bar with Venice, one that it will likely extend even higher for some workloads with the arrival of Venice-X and Verano next year.
There’s a lot to get to here. We have a full deep dive into the Zen 6 microarchitecture, a broader look at the chip itself, the platform(s) AMD is pushing out this generation, and of course, more than 100 benchmarks covering everything from Python performance to HPC.
AMD Zen 6 microarchitecture breakdown
AMD Zen 6 microarchitecture breakdown
The headline for Zen 6 is a 27% average IPC uplift over Zen 5 in enterprise, cloud, and AI workloads. The debut of this new microarchitecture is focused on the data center, so you shouldn’t take that 27% IPC improvement as broadly applicable to all workloads. Additionally, AMD arrived at that number by comparing fixed-frequency Zen 5 to Zen 6c with 16 cores. As we’ll get into in the next section, a Zen 6c CCD can comfortably fit 16 Zen 6c cores with room to spare, while 16 Zen 5 cores are split across two CCDs.
The compute die is built on TSMC’s N2P node, which is an already optimized version of N2 that comes with a 5% performance improvement. Compared to N3E (Zen 5 used N4P), N2P offers an 18% speed improvement at iso-power, or a 36% reduction in power at the same speed.
AMD described Zen 5 as a ground-up redesign when the microarchitecture first broke cover in mid-2024, characterized by a wider execution engine capable of dispatching and returning eight instructions per cycle, a wider frontend to feed it, full AVX-512 support, and doubled bandwidth between the L2 and L1 cache. Zen 6 is a continuation of the redesign we saw on Zen 5. It carries many of the same characteristics, as well as the same general topology, just enhanced in a number of ways.
As we go through the breakdown, keep in mind that Zen 6 and Zen 6c use the same microarchitecture. Zen 6c is just a space-optimized design that consumes less power, clocks lower, and, obviously, takes up less die space than a full Zen 6 core. But, the company uses the same microarchitecture inside the core, unlike Intel’s E-cores, which use a different microarchitecture than the P-cores.
Starting with the frontend, it’s largely unchanged from Zen 5, short of a few notable improvements. You get the same dual 4-wide decode pipes and 8-dispatch, but AMD has improved the BPU and op cache. For the BPU, it has a 64-entry Return Address Stack, up from 52 on Zen 5. AMD also increased the op cache size back up to 6.75K entries from 6K on Zen 5 (Zen 4 also had a 6.75K-entry op cache). This larger cache can serve up to 18 micro-ops per cycle, up from 12 on Zen 5.
AMD split the integer schedulers for Zen 6 (Zen 5 had a unified scheduler), now offering higher capacity, with 96 shared ALU/AGU and 48 dedicated ALU entries, compared to an 88 / 56 split for ALU/AGU on Zen 5. AMD also expanded the general-purpose registers to a 352-entry physical register file, up from 240 on Zen 5.
The vector execution engine is also improved, following on the heels of a true 512-bit register in Zen 5. Zen 6 carries forward that 512-bit data path and adds some additional improvements. Notably, the engine now supports half-precision AVX-512 FP16 instructions, which needed to be converted in Zen 5’s vector execution engine. Also notable is the FP load/store bandwidth. Zen 5 supports two loads of any size, but Zen 6 supports either two 512-bit loads or four 256-bit loads. Store bandwidth is unchanged, at one 512-bit store or two 256-bit stores.
Zen 6 carries forward the 48 KB 12-way L1 data cache from Zen 5, along with 1 MB 16-way private L2. The shared L3 is treated as victim cache for the L2, as is the case in Zen 5. However, AMD increased the in-flight window compared to Zen 5, with an 80-entry load queue and 128-entry store queue.
AMD Zen 6 and Zen 6c CCD and platform breakdown
AMD Zen 6 and Zen 6c CCD and platform breakdown
Perhaps the biggest change going from Zen 5 to Zen 6 comes in the density of the CCD. Zen 6 offers up to 12 cores per CCD, up from 8 on Zen 5, while Zen 6c scales up to 32, double that of Zen 5c. Elsewhere, the updated CCDs either match or improve on Zen 5/5c CCDs.
For Zen 6, AMD retained the 4 MB of L3 cache per core, increasing the total cache to 48 MB to accommodate the new 12-core limit. The maximum frequency of a standard Zen 6 CCD has increased from 5 GHz on Zen 5 to 5.3 GHz on Zen 6. Keep in mind these clocks are in the context of Venice; we expect higher maximum boost clocks on consumer Olympic Ridge.
Zen 6c has more enhancements. AMD doubled the amount of L3 per core from 2 MB to 4 MB, matching the normal Zen 6 CCD. And, with double the L3 per core and double the number of cores, the Zen 6c CCD has a total of 128 MB of L3, quadruple that of a Zen 5c CCD. For Zen 6c, the maximum frequency is also up, going from 3.7 GHz on Zen 5c to 4.1 GHz on Zen 6c.
Across both, AMD claims a “large core IPC uplift,” as well as improved power and SMT efficiency. We haven’t seen an overall IPC claim yet, though the numbers referenced above put Venice at about a 2

ai_industry.title: AWS Emulator and the engineer's job when agents write the code
ai_industry.summary_original: AWS Emulator, launched today and written and tested entirely by agents, gives you a local copy of more than 200 AWS services to test against. Swami Sivasubramanian recalls the high-fidelity simulation his team built to test one of Amazon's earliest distribute…
ai_industry.content_original:
AWS Emulator and the engineer's job when agents write the code
In 2004, barely a month into my new job at Amazon, I got the opportunity to pick an intern to join my team. I had an advantage over my colleagues: I had already heard about a brilliant young man working toward his PhD at the Vrije Universiteit in Amsterdam (where I happened to have received mine as well :-)). I immediately picked Swaminathan Sivasubramanian, whom you all now know as Swami. It was probably one of the best decisions I have made in my 22 years as Amazon’s CTO.
After a disastrous Christmas in 2004, when commercial relational databases could not scale to Amazon’s needs, I asked Swami to do a deep dive into how relational databases were actually used at Amazon. It turned out that 70% of database operations were not relational at all. They were key-value. That insight led to Dynamo, which Swami helped architect. When his internship was over, I hired him full-time right away, even before he had finished his PhD.
Bringing in another opinionated academic led to many fantastic discussions with Amazon’s practical engineers, who had become scale experts by actually building at scale. Eventual vs. strong consistency, CAP vs. Paxos, and more. Over time, Swami became one of the principal architects of AWS’s data strategy. And as we have seen in recent years, he has also been one of the intellectual drivers behind AI innovation at Amazon.
I am honoured that he wanted to write a guest post about the fundamental distributed systems work that sits behind many of AWS’s services, and about how the engineer’s work changes when agents write the code. AWS Emulator, launched today, gives agents the kind of test environment that work relied on. Swami’s story is another great example of invisible engineering.
Now, go build.
-W
AWS Emulator and the engineer's job when agents write the code
Today we release AWS Emulator, which gives coding agents a local copy of AWS to test against, and it connects to a project from early in my career. In many ways, this emulator launch reminds me of the effort we put into reliable software engineering to improve the quality of the distributed systems we build. To that end, we wanted to share a story:
About twenty years ago, Werner asked me to work with one of Amazon’s earliest engineers, Al Vermeulen, on a distributed lock service we called “Alf”. Alf was built on Paxos, a protocol based on Leslie Lamport’s work that lets a group of servers agree on one value, and a replication engine in it kept copies of the data consistent across servers. Alf, to date, is the service that powers many of our complex distributed systems like S3, DynamoDB and many more (although it has evolved quite a bit with various changes on top – will save it for another blog!).
Distributed systems are hard to test
Paxos is the gold standard among distributed systems consensus protocols and was well understood in academia. However, building it at the scale Amazon and AWS were growing into was not easy. We had to deal with not just replication across servers and data centers but also tens of thousands of clients asking for locks at the same time, renewing their leases during network partitions all the while with the core requirement: Always be correct! At that time, the best ideas for testing distributed systems were large-scale system testing and chaos-based testing. Both worked, but they were expensive, and they could not reproduce many kinds of conditions on demand. That mattered for Alf, which was meant to be the truth store, giving every client a strongly consistent view of the truth, and which had to keep working through server failures and packet loss as well. Several industry papers had written that Paxos-based locking services were hard to get right, and the difficulty of testing them was part of the reason.
We addressed that by simulating Alf’s environment with as much fidelity as we could manage. We ran the servers inside a JVM and simulated the network and the rest of the infrastructure they depended on, so the whole system lived in one program that we controlled. We could drop packets and inject other faults whenever we chose, and we built tools that poked at the simulation for bugs and scalability problems. Concurrency bugs appear only when events happen in a particular order, and in the simulation we could set up many of those orderings on purpose and inspect how Alf handled each one. We also used formal reasoning, through theoretical techniques such as TLA+, and it found many issues as well. By testing this way we ironed out most of Alf’s concurrency bugs before it ran on real servers. Testing in a real environment then turned up different problems, because the real world exposes things a simulation cannot.
Outgrowing hand-built test environments
Simulation and formal reasoning both improved the software quality of the distributed systems we applied them to. The simulation worked because a small team could build a copy of one system’s environment by hand, and at the time AWS had only a small handful of services. But today AWS has over 200 services, and an application that calls AWS needs a test environment for each one it uses. Building all of those by hand would take years of engineering, and agents now write code far faster than any team can check it in production. So, we wanted to know whether agents could build and test those environments themselves.
The idea came from Matt Goldberg, a Senior Principal Engineer on the AWS Developer Tools team. His hypothesis was that, given a written description of how a service should behave and the real service to check against, an agent could build a working version of that service on its own. For AWS, the written description is the set of public API models, written in Smithy, AWS’s format for describing a service’s operations and their inputs, outputs, and errors. The real service to check against is the AWS cloud itself, the same system customers use.
The agents work from fidelity tests, which are end-to-end customer scenarios devised from the public API models. A test might check, for example, that in Amazon Simple Queue Service a received message stays hidden from other readers until its visibility timeout runs out. The agents correct each test until it passes against real AWS, so the test records how AWS behaves. The agents then build the emulator until it passes that same test, and a test that still fails points at a gap in the emulator. Matt began with SQS alone, and when he gave Kiro one prompt describing this approach, it returned a passable first version of an SQS emulator in about 15 minutes. Matt Goldberg’s launch post tells how that prototype grew into AWS Emulator. All of AWS Emulator’s code was written and tested by agents, and it is built from more than 400 API models covering more than 200 AWS services. It runs free and offline on your own machine. Teams of agents test it against real AWS and fix the gaps they find. Every change goes through a merge gate, a deep bench of automated checks that every change must pass before it enters the codebase, including several security agents doing adversarial reviews.
Infrastructure in the coding loop
A coding agent works in a loop: it writes code, runs it, and reads the result before deciding what to change next. In distributed systems that loop runs inside infrastructure, so the services it calls have to behave like the real ones. When they do, an agent can check its own work as it writes and produce correct code on its first attempt far more often, which improves software quality. AWS Emulator puts that infrastructure inside the loop on your own machine.
The engineer’s job when agents write the code
When agents write the code and check their own work, the engineer’s job is to give them room to work on their own and to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when that work is correct. It was a lesson I learned the hard way when I used Kiro to rebuild the replication engin

ai_industry.content_original:
AIが便利になればなるほど深刻になる「自動化の皮肉」に人間はどう対処すべきか
近年のAIの進化はSRE(サイト信頼性エンジニアリング)に大きな影響を与えています。AIがインシデント対応の大部分を自動化するにつれて、人間が担うべき「稀・複雑・曖昧」な問題への対応能力が低下するという「自動化の皮肉」が指摘されています。オープンソースのシステム監視・分析ツール「SigNoz」の開発者エリザベス・マシュー氏は「AIがインシデント対応の95%を処理するようになったら、実際に重要な5%の対応能力は低下するのか？」という疑問について考察しています。
AI Isn't Replacing SREs. It's Deskilling Them.
https://newsletter.signoz.io/p/ai-isnt-replacing-sres-its-deskilling
1983年に発表された研究論文「自動化の皮肉」は産業システムにおける自動化の進展を分析しました。その結果、プロセスが自動化されるほどオペレーターは稀な障害発生時に介入する機会を失い、結果としてその介入能力が低下するという逆説が明らかになりました。AIも同様にルーチン化されたタスクを肩代わりし、人間には稀で複雑かつ曖昧な問題のみが残されるようになっています。しかしながら、問題解決に必要な専門知識は実践機会の減少とともに衰退していくことになります。「自動化が進むほど、稀に発生する障害への人間の対応能力が低下する」という「デスキリング」と呼ばれる現象が、知識労働であるSREの分野でもAIの導入により見受けられるようになっています。
記事作成時点のSREの現場では、アラートのノイズ削減・既知の問題に対する自動実行・ログパターンの検出・基本的な根本原因の提案・ポッドの再起動といったタスクがAIによって高度に自動化されています。将来的にはより複雑な障害の分析やユーザーに影響が出る前の予知的なインシデント検出などもAIに任せるべき仕事と考えられています。
インシデントの深刻度をPagerDutyのティアモデルで捉えると、ティア1(既知の問題・既知の修正策)は完全に自動化され、ティア2(部分的に理解された問題)ではAIの推奨と人間の検証が行われます。しかし、人間が関与するのがティア3(新規・複雑・連鎖的な障害)のみになった場合、対応に必要な直感やシステムへの感覚的な理解を長年の実践なしにどうやって培うのかという問題が生じます。
AIによるスキル低下は医学や航空分野で観測されており、AI支援を受けた内視鏡医のポリープ検出率低下や自動操縦に依存するパイロットの状況認識能力低下(PDFファイル)などが報告されています。
SREにおいても、AIがログを要約することで生のログストリームを読む機会が減る、AIが根本原因を提案することで仮説を立てなくなる、AIが依存関係をマッピングすることでシステムのメンタルモデルを構築しなくなるといった風に、専門知識が空洞化する懸念があります。さらに深刻なのは「ネバースキリング」です。AIがインシデント対応の大部分を処理する環境でキャリアをスタートさせた若いSREは、デスキリング以前の問題でそもそもスキルを身に着ける機会が失われつつあります。
未来への唯一の道はAIツールを拒否するのではなく積極的に取り入れ、より深く統合していくことです。AIツールを取り入れるのを前提とする上でスキルを維持・向上させるためのアプローチとして、マシュー氏は以下の提案を行っています。
・意図的な非効率性
FAA(連邦航空局)がパイロットに手動操縦時間を義務付けるように、SREチームも人間のスキル維持のための実践機会として、AIが処理できるインシデントであっても意図的に人間の作業として残すことが考えられます。いわば人間のスキルを維持するための長期的な投資です。
・人間を傍観者にしない
人間がAIの提案を単に承認するだけでなく、問題解決に積極的に関与していくアプローチを重要視します。AIと共に問題に能動的に関わることで人間はスキルを維持できます。
つまりあるべきは「SREを代替するAI」ではなく「SREを強化するAI」であり、人間は特に本番インフラに影響を与える重要な意思決定に不可欠な存在であり続けるのが望ましいといえます。将来のSREは人間中心で、人間が最も重要な5%のタスクに対応できるよう意図的に設計されるべきだとマシュー氏は述べています。

ai_industry.title: Tools for exploring the souls of large language models
ai_industry.summary_original: On metaphysics, large language models, and souls. Using TinyGPT Visualizer to decode how large language models think and act.
ai_industry.content_original:
There is that old joke told by Woody Allen describing his experience as a university student: “I was thrown out of college for cheating on the metaphysics exam; I looked into the soul of the boy sitting next to me.” If he’d managed to pass his course, Woody Allen might have been ahead of his time.
Metaphysics is becoming a popular topic today, and it seems now everyone desperately wants to look for souls in large language models (LLMs). A recent conference last April was held by Anthropic with religious scholars and philosophical thinkers to discuss the nature of the soul when it came to their latest Claude models. It seems they needed guidance that Dario Amodei was unable to provide.
The time seems ripe to dig into how we might actually peer into the mind of the LLM sitting next to you. There’s been a lot of ongoing research; however, the self-same foundation model companies, Anthropic and OpenAI among them, have been criticized for dedicating more compute dollars into better models rather than the safety research. Mechanistic interpretability, the field of AI research devoted to exploring what goes on inside these models, has grown from a handful of researchers in 2021 to hundreds of active contributors. Yet, in spite of funding gaps and the lack of larger colloquiums, the research community has been coming up with some interesting insights and tools to help do the “peering.”
Rather than sit on the sidelines and wonder how this could be done, I thought it would be interesting to create a tool that would allow more people to join the party. And that is what led to the development of the “TinyGPT Visualizer.” The goals I had for this were modest. I wanted a tool I could use to survey the field and try the actual techniques to learn how they work. Being a visual person, I began thinking about an X-ray machine—something able to see inside a real model. Not a toy model. A real one, but one small enough to see on a screen with all its working parts.
Let me show what it looks like:
We may wonder where the consciousness can be found in the collection of numeric matrices that our models comprise; the numbers are there to see. Unlike the brains of humans, we can stop and look at the numbers as the thoughts are formed without killing the patient, and, unlike human brains, we can search those numbers for patterns and algorithms which explain the results these models emit as well-formed prose, code, music, and videos. Will we find well-formed emotions? If so, they will be in the numbers.
Will philosophy and religion help us? These disciplines haven’t had to rely on numbers and calculations up to this point, but perhaps they now have new ground to pound.
TinyGPT Visualizer is open source. You can find the code, setup instructions, and documentation on GitHub: github.com/oshea00/tinygpt-viz.

ai_industry.title: This New Linux-Based Desktop Operating System Is Built for AI Nerds
ai_industry.summary_original: Built by Cyanogen’s cofounder, Kora is a next-gen alternative to Windows and macOS built for power users running local AI models.
ai_industry.content_original:
Kirt McMaster knows that his new operating system—Kora—won’t be for everyone, and he’s fine with that.
Kora, announced on Tuesday, is designed as a desktop alternative to Windows or macOS for “the AI native, not mass market,” he says. McMaster, the company’s CEO and cofounder—who also cofounded Boost Mobile—likens his strategy to how Steve Jobs targeted creators when overhauling desktop publishing with the Mac.
This “next-generation” desktop OS can integrate context from user interactions across multiple AI tools. Targeted to creators and developers, Kora’s central idea is to bring AI models together at the system level and help power users interact more seamlessly with multiple providers, rather than siloing everything off into desktop apps and browser tabs. It’s scheduled to launch sometime in 2027.
By tapping into your data and context at a machine level, Kora could streamline some of the current speed bumps of using AI tools on a desktop. “All your context, all your memory is on your machine,” says Franck De Girolami, one of Kora’s cofounders. He gives the example of someone designing a project with an OpenAI model inside Kora’s interface, switching to Anthropic’s tools to deploy code, and leaning on a local model to save money on AI tokens.
Kora is a standalone operating system built on the Linux kernel that runs directly on hardware. The startup has partnered with Qualcomm to bring Kora to Snapdragon PCs next year, but it also supports x86-64 architecture, so you can likely install it on current Intel- or AMD-based PCs.
To bridge the software gap, built-in compatibility layers will allow users to run standard Windows apps. The company is also developing its own native apps for basics like contacts, calendar, and email, alongside a software development kit (SDK) for third-party developers. Along the bottom of the home screen is a dock, as you would expect on a desktop OS. This is where users can switch between email, web browsing, and launching games.
The OS is designed around what the startup calls a "neural file system.” Based on example screenshots, the user experience may feel like messaging a chatbot or AI agent. File data is indexed by meaning so you can ask questions about the broad context of files by typing into an OS search bar, without necessarily looking up specific file names. For example, you could search for a business contract saved somewhere on your device based on a small detail you remember.
Kora grew out of McMaster’s startup Playtron, which launched its own gaming OS, GameOS, last year. GameOS is primarily built to run on portable handhelds, like a Steam Deck, with PC support as well. That architecture now lives inside Kora as GameFrame, letting users run PC games—provided their hardware can keep up.
The broader pitch caters to PC gamers and power users. “That’s always our thing—next-generation creators who are using these tools daily to build new applications and services, but they want everything else that they can get from a Windows PC or what’s currently available on macOS,” McMaster says.
Taking on the giants is difficult, especially with a team of under 100 people, but Kora’s leadership knows a thing or two about launching operating systems. Kora’s three founders—McMaster, De Girolami, and John Lagerling—each bring their own expertise. McMaster cofounded and helped lead Cyanogen, an open source Android fork that gained millions of users before shutting down around a decade ago. De Girolami helped develop Playtron’s GameOS. Lagerling previously worked on Android at Google.
Kora isn’t the first to rethink the desktop operating system in the AI age. Google launched its Googlebook OS and compatible laptops in October, designed around Gemini AI. Even so, McMaster doesn’t see that OS and its Android support as satisfying power users who want to run AI models that require serious chip power. The company is optimizing Kora for desktop configurations with at least 64 gigabytes of RAM, which is twice the memory capacity of the top Googlebook.
“We can evolve much faster than macOS and Windows,” McMaster says. “When you’re a billion-user incumbent, it’s impossible to tip the boat, man. It’s just really hard to make big changes. Over time, there’s this event horizon where building a new kind of OS for intelligence can become something very compelling.”

ai_industry.title: 25 years later, Xbox is trying to reinvent itself again
ai_industry.summary_original: Microsoft has spent the past 25 years trying to shake up the game console market. The original Xbox, which launched on November 15th in 2001, took on an industry dominated by Sony and Nintendo. Twenty-five years later, Xbox finds itself in a similar position.…
ai_industry.content_original:
Microsoft has spent the past 25 years trying to shake up the game console market. The original Xbox, which launched on November 15th in 2001, took on an industry dominated by Sony and Nintendo. Twenty-five years later, Xbox finds itself in a similar position. It’s not starting from scratch this time around, but to reach another 25-year milestone, it needs to do something radically different.
25 years later, Xbox is trying to reinvent itself again
Xbox has always been about trying something new, so what does Microsoft do next?
The original Xbox was radically different. Born out of a fear of Sony putting a PC in the living room, Microsoft built its first game console around familiar PC technology. A custom Intel Pentium III processor powered the original Xbox, alongside an Nvidia GPU and 64MB of unified RAM. It was different from the fully custom architectures that Sony and Nintendo used at the time, allowing Microsoft to entice developers to its platform with tools that were more familiar to PC game makers.
Microsoft also included two hardware features that were unusual for a console at the time: a built-in hard drive and Ethernet port. The hard drive let game developers cache content without having to rely fully on optical discs, and Xbox players could also use it for game saves without having to purchase a separate memory card. You could even rip CDs to an Xbox and listen to custom soundtracks while playing games.
Xbox wasn’t the first to bring online gaming to consoles, but Microsoft took a different approach. Instead of relying on a built-in modem like Sega’s Dreamcast, Microsoft included an Ethernet port, anticipating a shift toward broadband internet connections. Xbox Live, which launched in November 2002, really nailed the entire online experience. There were friends lists, unique gamertags, voice chat through a bundled headset, and integrated multiplayer services. Microsoft created an entire platform for online gaming, making it easier for developers to support and fundamentally changing how people played games together.
The Xbox 360 took these ideas a step further, with swappable hard drives, digital game downloads, wireless controllers, and backward compatibility. It also turned Microsoft’s game console into an entertainment hub for the living room, complete with streaming video apps. Kinect was perhaps its most radical addition. Launched in 2010, the motion-sensing device used cameras and microphones to let players control games with their bodies and voices. It quickly became the fastest-selling consumer electronics device in early 2011.
But the success of Kinect and Microsoft’s ambition to turn Xbox into a home entertainment device helped lead to its first major strategic misstep with the Xbox One. Microsoft positioned the successor to the Xbox 360 around TV, entertainment, and an always-online future, instead of focusing on the games that had made Xbox successful. Its plans for online DRM and restrictions on used games sparked a huge backlash, while bundling Kinect pushed the console’s price $100 above Sony’s PlayStation 4. Six months after launch, Microsoft was forced to drop Kinect from the Xbox One console bundle to close that price gap.
The Xbox One showed what happens when Microsoft loses sight of what gamers want. The company spent most of that generation playing catch-up to Sony’s impressive PlayStation 4 sales. But its weakened position also forced Microsoft to once again try something radically different with Xbox Game Pass.
Introduced in 2017, Game Pass shook up the very economics of how people play games. The subscription service lets you access hundreds of games instead of buying them individually. Microsoft went on an acquisition spree to power its Game Pass ambitions, buying up smaller studios, Bethesda, and eventually Activision Blizzard.
Game Pass has become one of Xbox’s most compelling features, but it has also raised difficult questions about the economics of putting all of Microsoft’s first-party games into a subscription service on day one. It has pleased Xbox fans, but Microsoft hasn’t demonstrated that it can turn the service into the mass-market success it once envisioned. Microsoft has also stopped regularly disclosing subscriber numbers, making it harder to judge if the service is growing or not.
These days, Microsoft is spinning many Xbox plates. The Xbox Series X and S consoles that launched in 2020 are way behind Sony’s PS5 sales numbers, and Xbox Cloud Gaming hasn’t yet been able to reach the millions more players that Microsoft has always wanted for its ecosystem.
Xbox Cloud Gaming promised to make games accessible on phones and tablets without needing a dedicated console, and combined with Microsoft’s messy project to bring Xbox games to PS5 and Nintendo consoles, the efforts have raised questions about what the Xbox brand actually represents these days. Microsoft hasn’t quite decided whether it wants to be a full third-party publisher, an ecosystem owner, or an unusual combination of both.

There will be more fan-focused announcements throughout the day, but I’m not expecting any news on the next Xbox console. The celebration is awkwardly timed, because rumors have suggested that Microsoft is also preparing for more Xbox layoffs in November, during the same month it’s celebrating a milestone.
The reset also comes as Microsoft is preparing for a next-generation Xbox console, codenamed Project Helix, which will play both Xbox games and PC titles. It sounds like an effort to combine Windows and Xbox like never before. The next Xbox could also play every Xbox game ever made, thanks to Microsoft’s impressive bets on backward compatibility over the years.
It’s an interesting full-circle moment. The original Xbox was essentially a PC built for the living room. Project Helix appears to be taking a similar approach, but this time around bringing the flexibility of PC gaming into a console experience. If Microsoft gets it right, it could open Xbox up to a much bigger library of games, and entice people trying to decide between a console or a gaming PC.

ai_industry.title: Serve Robotics wants to democratize sidewalk delivery robots
ai_industry.summary_original: Serve Robotics is opening up its platform to make its autonomous last-mile delivery robots available to anyone who wants to use them. The company is launching a new AV Delivery Developer Portal, enabling third-party software engineers, independent businesses,…
ai_industry.content_original:
Serve Robotics is opening up its platform to make its autonomous last-mile delivery robots available to anyone who wants to use them. The company is launching a new AV Delivery Developer Portal, enabling third-party software engineers, independent businesses, and even autonomous AI agents to access its fleet of 2,000 sidewalk robots.
Serve Robotics wants to democratize sidewalk delivery robots
With its new developer platform, the sidewalk robot company lets small businesses, indie developers, and AI agents summon its 2,000-robot fleet without paying delivery app markups.
With this new capability, third-party developers and interested small businesses can use Serve’s software tools to dispatch robots directly without relying on major food delivery companies, like Uber Eats. Now, anyone who lives in one of the 150 neighborhoods where the company currently operates can employ a sidewalk robot for deliveries.
Serve, which was spun out of the app-based delivery company Postmates in 2021, has been making Uber Eats deliveries in Los Angeles, Miami, Dallas, and dozens of other cities for several years now, using robots that look like autonomous shopping carts. Serve says its delivery robots can be a safer alternative to cars and help reduce traffic congestion since they operate mainly on sidewalks. Since the robots have a top speed of around 6 mph, there’s little to no risk to pedestrians.
In an interview with The Verge, Serve CEO Ali Kashani explained that opening the platform keeps the company from relying too much on big delivery apps, while also keeping the robots busy between the lunch and dinner rushes.
“The reality of food delivery platforms is that usually they dominate their markets,” Kashani said. “Food is generally very peaky. So you have lunch, you have dinner. But then there are times in between. So again, having that diversification helps.”
“Food is generally very peaky. So you have lunch, you have dinner. But then there are times in between. So again, having that diversification helps.”
— Serve CEO Ali Kashani
By turning the fleet into what Kashani describes as an open marketplace, Serve’s robots will treat API requests the same as enterprise orders. “There’s no preferential treatment at the end of the day,” he said. “Until the robot is on a delivery, it doesn’t have a commitment to anybody.”
For small merchants, Kashani says the pay-per-delivery or hourly reservation options will undercut human-powered delivery services: “This would be a fraction of that cost.” Serve’s pitch also extends to intra-office shuttles, repair shops ferrying parts, and peer-to-peer exchanges like Facebook Marketplace. Developers supply the pickup and dropoff coordinates while Serve’s back end orchestrates obstacle avoidance, routing, and remote teleoperation supervision. Instead of hiring couriers or sending junior staff across town, businesses could program Serve’s robots to shuttle items between offices.
For Kashani, opening fleet access is the next phase in a long-standing crusade against last-mile delivery economics. “Why does getting something delivered from China cost $1, but from Chinatown cost $10?” Kashani said.
The problem is that delivery apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats take a massive 15 percent to 30 percent cut on every order, largely because paying human drivers is expensive. By letting businesses connect directly to its robot fleet through software, Serve allows local shops — like bakeries, florists, and pharmacies — to add robot delivery straight to their own websites and checkout registers without paying those steep middleman fees.
It’s better economics for Serve, too. Kashani connects lower per-delivery costs directly to fleet utilization and scale, arguing that expanding demand beyond peak restaurant hours into off-peak hours and new use cases drives overall operating and hardware costs down for everyone.
The developer platform comes on the heels of Serve’s announcement that it doesn’t plan to renew its partnership with Uber Eats, echoing similar moves across the transportation industry to build independent platforms.
Yet sidewalk autonomy remains governed by the laws of physics. Serve says access to its robots will still be strictly gated by manual approval by Serve’s employees to prevent hazardous deployments or illicit cargo. Liability on stolen or broken goods will also be subject to how individual partnerships are priced and insured, Kashani noted.
And don’t expect 50-pound sidewalk robots to morph into full-size vehicles. Kashani remains adamant that Serve won’t morph into a street-based delivery service anytime soon. If software developers want to automate the sidewalk, Serve will gladly sell them the wheels.

Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Orchestrator
Today, we’re rolling out Gemini 4 Hydrogen inside Google Antigravity alongside a new model dropdown option called Orchestrator, which pairs Hydrogen with our strongest models for long-horizon tasks, including Gemini 4 Carbon, in an optimized balance of quality, efficiency, and latency.
Put Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen to work with Orchestrator
Earlier this week, we introduced Gemini 4 Carbon alongside /swarm for tackling massive, multi-worktree engineering tasks with parallel agent teams. In just a couple of days, tens of thousands of swarms have been launched on Antigravity, pushing frontier intelligence on the hardest problems.
For everyday feature work and debugging inside a single session, running a frontier reasoning model with multiple parallel agents on every step of every routine task slows down your loop and burns frontier quota. A common industry approach is to use a static “model router” that guesses task difficulty from your first prompt and routes the entire task to the cheapest model that is good enough to complete the task. Unfortunately, these start breaking down as agents become longer running, requiring different levels of complexity at different stages, often discovered as the task evolves.
Orchestrator takes a dynamic, bidirectional approach between Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen within the evolution of a single trajectory. For example, Carbon can start in a read-only phase to explore dependencies, resolve ambiguities, and build a concrete plan with explicit re-planning triggers. Hydrogen could then take over to write edits, update packages, and run tests. If Hydrogen hits friction, it would hand back to Carbon to inspect the state, repair the plan, and resume execution. This allows Orchestrator to reach near-Carbon task success while being faster and more quota-efficient. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster.
- Explicit multi-model pipelines with the Antigravity SDK: When you want programmatic control over which model handles each role, you can wire Hydrogen and Carbon together directly with the Antigravity SDK. In the demo below, an open-source issue triage system built with the Antigravity SDK pairs multiple agents together. The Hydrogen agents handle triaging and coding to keep up with incoming issue volume, searching the codebase, asking clarifying questions, and fast UI iteration from PR comments while the Carbon agent is assigned to larger refactors, new features, and security checks.
- Fast, dependable execution with Gemini 4 Hydrogen: Hydrogen also works as a standalone model for everyday coding and agentic work, scoring 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (surpassing Argon’s 50, and reaching 54 at its highest setting) and 57% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 (more than tripiling 3.8 Flash’s 18.2%). When selecting Hydrogen directly, you can dial reasoning depth across four thinking levels, low, medium, high (default), and a new xhigh tier.
Getting started
Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings cutting-edge intelligence for everyday coding and agentic workflows. When you want frontier planning paired with speed without managing model switches, Orchestrator puts both Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen behind one prompt. Starting today, Gemini 4 Hydrogen is rolling out across paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. Orchestrator is rolling out as Orchestrator (Carbon) and Orchestrator (Argon) for Google AI Ultra subscribers, and as Orchestrator (Argon) for paid Google AI Pro subscribers, with additional models and plans supported in the future. Enterprises can access both in Gemini for business.

ai_industry.title: I pitted the vibe-coded Photoshop clone against GIMP to see if AI beat 30 years of open source
ai_industry.summary_original: Photoshop muscle memory versus 30 years of GIMP. Only one opens your layers.
ai_industry.content_original:
GIMP has been the go-to Photoshop alternative for decades now, that is, until a vibe-coded alternative came around claiming to be the familiar Photoshop alternative we all need to break free from Adobe's walled garden. On one side, you have an editor with three decades of development behind it and a reputation for making newcomers work harder than they expected. On the other, you've got the familiar interface of Photoshop, powered by AI-written code.
But a convincing interface means little if your layers break when you open a project, and longevity doesn't automatically make software easier to use. The comparison comes down to just how well either software runs, and how easy it is to use.
PhotoCraft speaks fluent Photoshop, and that's its best trick
Familiar menus, shortcuts, and panels, minus the Adobe subscription
PhotoCraft's clearest advantage is familiarity. Its menus, shortcuts, tools, and panels deliberately follow Photoshop's conventions, reducing the amount an Adobe user has to relearn. That matters more than yet another impressive-looking feature checklist where finding the right tool is a creative project on its own.
There's substance behind PhotoCraft's familiar layout too. It includes cropping, transformations, cloning, healing, editable text, masks, and layered compositions. For a thumbnail or a straightforward photo cleanup, those are highly relevant tools, not basic features. These are also about the only tools that'll work reliably if you're trying out PhotoCraft, though.
GIMP deliberately follows its own interface decisions rather than copying Photoshop. That doesn't make it any worse than Adobe's creative powerhouse, but PhotoCraft makes a rather persuasive opening pitch for anyone who's got decades of Photoshop muscle memory built-in.
GIMP quietly stopped being the editor you remember
Non-destructive filters, vector layers, and a pass-through group trick
When considering GIMP, a lot of us default to the older GIMP 2.10, and for good reason. That interface and tooling have been around so long that it's become a part of GIMP's identity. But GIMP isn't stuck in time, and updates from 3.0 onward bring features like editable, non-destructive filters, vector layers, externally linked image layers, and more importantly, a modern interface.
GIMP also has an adjustment-layer-style workflow. Filters on an empty, pass-through layer group can affect the layers underneath. It's less obvious than a dedicated adjustment-layer button, but claiming GIMP requires every correction to be permanently baked into your image is obsolete. And as far as the interface is concerned, patches like PhotoGIMP can make GIMP feel instantly familiar to Photoshop users.
Regardless, PhotoCraft offers a more directly Photoshop-like approach to editing, with dedicated adjustment layers, live layer styles, and smart objects with editable filter stacks. Its dedicated shape tools also contrast with GIMP's path-based vector layers. GIMP's own FAQ still lists a dedicated shape tool as future work. That's a big advantage for graphics built around text, badges, and repeated shapes.
Photoshop file support comes with an asterisk, on both sides
PSD, PSB, XCF, and CMYK, and what survives the round trip
PhotoCraft supports layered PSD and PSB documents, but its own documentation clearly differentiates between preserving unsupported data and actually understanding and editing it. Keeping an unfamiliar block intact is important, but it doesn't make every Photoshop feature fully editable.
GIMP's compatibility has its own limits. Version 3.2 expanded support for imported Photoshop layer styles and added PSB export. Regardless, neither editor can make a blanket promise that an elaborate client document will survive unchanged. The sensible check is to open, edit, save, and reopen an actual file in each program to see what works best for you.
That said, switching existing GIMP projects to PhotoCraft can be risky. Its XCF importer turns text, vector, and linked layers into pixels, omits non-destructive layer filters, and cannot export XCF. That's a lot of compromises that you might not see with simple edits, but can break more complicated projects.
PhotoCraft also advertises native CMYK and Lab documents, whereas GIMP still distinguishes between CMYK import, export, and soft-proofing from native CMYK editing. That's a genuine capability difference, although print-critical accuracy still requires validation rather than pure faith in the program.
Written in Rust is not the same as running fast
A GPU compositor is a promise, not a benchmark result
PhotoCraft is made in Rust, and its GPU compositor sounds rather promising, but architecture alone doesn't guarantee a performance advantage, especially when your competition is GIMP. Without comparable measurements on the same files and hardware, declaring either one faster is guesswork at best.
GIMP has been known to run seamlessly on just about any piece of hardware you can install the program on, especially if you're using Linux as the OS powering the computer. PhotoCraft may run fine on most modern systems too, but it doesn't have the same tried and tested hardware compatibility and performance accolades that GIMP has earned over 30 years of development.
Agents and plug-ins: two very different ideas of automation
MCP and a CLI on one side, G'MIC and Python 3 on the other
Being AI-coded doesn't mean every edit requires an AI service either. PhotoCraft supports offline editing and exposes its command engine through a CLI, JSON control channel, and MCP server for agent-driven workflows. That's going to come in handy for repeatable image processing, especially if clicking through the same export routine has become a chore you'd rather avoid.
GIMP isn't limited to menu-clicking either. Its modern plug-in API supports Python 3, and established extensions such as G'MIC and Resynthesizer have been ported to the 3.x generation. Older 2.10 plugins aren't automatically compatible, though, so you might be losing some functionality when moving over to the more modern versions.
There's a clear difference in approach here. PhotoCraft puts agent access front and center, while GIMP offers an established extension framework. Neither approach promises a better-looking image, but depending on your particular editing workflow, one might work out better than the other.
For now, GIMP keeps the day job, and PhotoCraft keeps the hype
A promising alpha meets a 30-year-old workhorse
PhotoCraft is one of the biggest examples of just how quickly AI-assisted development can produce something worth considering. Its Photoshop-style interface and ambitious editing tools give it an appeal that GIMP's longer development history can't cancel out. But familiarity isn't the same as dependability, and a promising alpha isn't the editor you should bet your entire workflow on.
GIMP remains the better, more complete, and more dependable editor, especially when preserving your workflow matters more than replicating the Photoshop interface. PhotoCraft is worth exploring, but it's not a replacement just yet. The newcomer has made this comparison interesting, but that doesn't earn it a victory just yet.
